title: Many-to-Many Relations
description: Compare implicit vs explicit many-to-many relations in Prisma and learn when to choose an explicit junction table.

data.text: A **Many-to-Many (M:N) relation** connects records where each entity can link to multiple instances of the other (e.g. `Post` and `Tag`, `Student` and `Course`). Prisma supports two ways to model M:N relations: **implicit** and **explicit**.

cards.title: Implicit Many-to-Many
cards.description: Prisma automatically creates and manages a hidden join table (`_PostToTag`) behind the scenes without defining a model in schema.prisma.
cons: Cannot store additional metadata on the relationship (e.g. `assignedAt`, `role`)

cards.title: Explicit Many-to-Many
cards.description: You define the junction table as an explicit model in schema.prisma with its own foreign keys and custom fields.
pros: Can store timestamps, status, permissions on the join record
Full control over physical database indexes

data.title: Implicit M:N Definition
data.content: Simply add array fields on both models.

data.title: Explicit M:N Definition with Metadata
data.content: Useful for memberships where you need to track `role` and `joinedAt`.
data.code:
model Team {
  id          String           @id @default(uuid())
  name        String
  memberships TeamMembership[]
}

model User {
  id          String           @id @default(uuid())
  name        String
  memberships TeamMembership[]
}

model TeamMembership {
  id        String   @id @default(uuid())
  teamId    String   @map("team_id")
  userId    String   @map("user_id")
  role      String   @default("MEMBER") // Metadata field
  joinedAt  DateTime @default(now())    // Metadata field

  team      Team     @relation(fields: [teamId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  user      User     @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  @@unique([teamId, userId])
  @@index([teamId])
  @@index([userId])
}

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use implicit M:N when you only need to associate IDs without extra columns.
Use explicit M:N as soon as the relationship requires metadata like `role`, `createdAt`, or `status`.
Always include composite unique constraints on junction tables.
